What's under the roof

One roof, a row of booths

Every booth belongs to a different vendor, so the building changes week to week. Tap a heading to see what tends to be in it.

  • Hand-pieced quilts hung along the walls
  • Framed paintings and prints leaned up to flip through
  • Old advertising pieces, a tall Coca-Cola sign among them
  • Pink depression glass, priced right on the shelf
  • Teacups, saucers and a rose-patterned teapot
  • Glass mixing bowls and everyday kitchenware
  • Boxed games and small collectibles below
  • Oil lanterns with their glass chimneys intact
  • Wall-mounted metal sconces
  • Vintage desk lamps with fabric shades
  • A floor lamp switched on beside the quilts
  • Wood cabinets, cases and shelving along the walls
  • Wooden crates, trunks and baskets out on the floor
  • Painted cabinets and a hutch stacked with dishware

    Meet the owner

    Brenda's shop, and everybody's stuff

    Brenda Evenson has run this shop out of the same historic building on Railroad Ave since May 2016.

    It works like a small mall: independent vendors keep their own booths, so the building is really a couple dozen collections sitting side by side. Nobody hovers. People come in to kill twenty minutes and lose an hour.

    There's usually a cart of free treats parked by the door — cookies, whatever the neighbors sent over — and coffee inside when it's cold out. Customers have been mentioning that cart in reviews for ten years running.

    Come by

    Pull up on the porch side

    1. Park out front

      Angle in along the street. The porch with the barrels and the string lights is the one.

    2. Take the whole loop

      It runs back further than the storefront suggests, so give yourself more time than you think.

    3. Ask at the counter

      If you can't find it, say so — that's how things end up on the wanted list.
